course.title: Benign anal and perianal disorders
course.html:
Hemorrhoids

  • Due to dystrophic changes of venous wall (perianal veins) = varix of ano-rectal veins
  • Ano-rectal veinous stasis plays major role
  • Typical lesion is venous dilation at level of hemorrhoidal plexus (between superior hemorrhoidal vein and middle

and inferior hemorrhoidal sinus → meeting point of portal and caval system)

  • Internal hemorrhoids are painless (above pectinate line) → lack of sensory innervation
  • External hemorrhoids are painful (below pectinate line) → sensory innervation from inferior rectal nerve
  • - Mixed

Etiology

Primitive/ Essential H.

  • Can be due to hereditary predisposal, local irritation,

malnutrition

  • Are more common in families with background of

hernia and varix of lower limb

  • Can be associated with IBD (CD, UC)
  • Pregnancy → increased pressure and hormonal

changes

  • Low fiber-diet
  • Reading on toilet → impaired venous return

Secondary H.

  • Porto-caval anastomosis → any obstacle in their area (e.g., cirrhosis, rectal tumors or large pelvic tumors) → must

be ruled out

Clinical manifestation

  • Engorged anal mucosa easily traumatized → rectal bleeding (bright red due to high blood oxygen content)
  • Prolapse leads to soiling and mucus discharge → triggering pruritus and predisposes to incarceration and strangulation

Evolution of internal hemorrhoids

Grade I- Can reach anal canal during defecation without prolapse but can bleed
Grade IIGrade II- Hemorrhoids may protrude beyond anal verge with straining or defecating but reduce spontaneously
when straining ceases
Grade III- Hemorrhoids protrude spontaneously or with straining and require manual reduction
Grade IVGrade IV- Hemorrhoids chronically prolapse and cannot be reduced
- Usually contain internal and external components
- May present with acute thrombosis or strangulation

Complications

Natural evolution begins with anitis → spreading of inflammation into veins = hemorrhoidal phlebitis → dilation of affected veins → vein hypertrophy with reflex contracture of sphincter and irreducibility of hemorrhoidal thrombosis

  • spontaneous healing of thrombosed H. forms a cutaneous flap
  • Bleeding
  • Suppuration
  • Necrosis
  • Fissure
  • Ulcer
  • Phlebitis of portal branches

Diagnosis

  • Inspection with rectal exam
  • Flexible sigmoidoscopy → necessary to rule out inflammation or neoplasia
  • Pancolonoscopy is safer if pat. is > 40 y or unspecific symptoms

Treatment

Grade I

  • Usually symptoms relieved by better local hygiene, avoidance of excessive straining, balanced diet with fiber
  • Suppositories and ointments containing cortisone should be avoided on long term basis

Grade II

  • Conservative techniques (rubber-band ligation, sclerotherapy, infrared photocoagulation, carbon dioxide freezing,

heater probe)

  • Rubber band ligation is easy and cheap BUT can lead to severe perineal sepsis and even death

Grade III and IV

  • Failure of non-operative therapy and with significant symptoms → hemorrhoidectomy
  • 1) Simple thrombosed external hemorrhoids - excision in office under local anesthesia immediately after onset
  • Ultrasonic scissors, bipolar electrocoagulation, laser can be used for resection
  • Prior to surgery, subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis in valvular patients must be administered
  • 2) Stapled hemorrhoid surgery (Longo technique) = procedure of choice for prolapsed hemorrhoids
  • Purse-string suture placed with help of a plastic funnel-shaped device in mucosa and submucosa above dentate line

beneath anvil; stapler is placed and closed

  • Excess hemorrhoid tissue resected by circular scalpel of stapler
  • Hemostasis with interruption of blood supply is ensured by staple-line

Anal fissures

= radial tear affecting epithelium of anus

Causes

  • Usually caused by passage of bulky, dehydrated piece of stool in constipated patients
  • Iatrogenic
  • Self-inflicted (foreign bodies)
  • Trauma
  • Inflamed and fragile epithelium in diarrhea can also be affected by anal fissure

Chronic fissure

= persistent ulcerous lesion with granulation tissue-covered base and fibrotic margins

  • Typically situated on posterior midline (over 90%) and is usually hidden by skin tag
  • Fibers of internal anal sphincter can be visible

DD

  • CD, TBC, Syphilis, Carcinoma

Symptoms

  • Vicious circle pain-spasm-pain associated with constipation (withhold defacation)
  • Small bleedings smear stool surface

Physical exam

  • DRE difficult because of spasm
  • 1-2 % lidocaine gel and gentle spreading of anus can visualize sentinel tag which hides anal fissure

Treatment

Conservative

  • Acute fissures usually heal without any special help
  • Local hygiene and avoidance of constipation
  • Chronic fissures may not respond and need
  • Anesthetic gel
  • Warm local bath 5 min before and after defecation
  • 0.2 % nitroglycerin ointment in anal canal will also ameliorate blood flow
  • Local injection of botulinic toxin bears risk of recurrence after 3 months

Surgical

  • 1) Anal dilation procedure (Lord procedure) → rare nowadays
  • gentle, progressive anal dilatation (under spinal anesthesia) for several minutes, must allow insertion of 3 fingers,

but without tearing internal sphincter

  • 2) Partial lateral internal sphincterotomy (method of choice)
  • reduces tension in anus and allows fissure to heal
  • Closed technique (not preferred): inserting thin scalpel between sphincters and cutting only internal component
  • Open technique: segmental incision between two sphincters, internal sphincter is then dissected and radially cut
  • 3) In recurrent cases plastic procedures using flaps must be considered

Closed Open

Perirectal (anorectal) abscess

  • Arise from cryptitis caused by obstruction of mucus-secreting anal glands which drain into anal crypts

Different types according to its progress and anatomical spaces

  • Submucosal
  • Ischiorectal
  • Pelvirectal
  • Horseshoe shaped
  • Supralevator or pelvisubperitoneal

Signs and symptoms

  • Perianal discomfort, pruritus (fist signs)
  • Inflammatory → swelling, redness, tenderness, elevated temp. of overlying skin (calor, dolor, rubor, tugor)
  • Deep collections can alter general status, fever, chills, nausea
  • Pelvisubperitoneal abscesses can associate urinary signs, particularly dangerous as they spread to retroperitonum

Diagnosis

  • Endorectal and vaginal US
  • CT
  • DRE → protrusion of rectal wall

Complications

  • Perianal fistula

Treatment

  • Percutaneous punction and drainage
  • Proper drainage can only be performed under spinal anesthesia
  • Cavity must be thoroughly explored digitally, necrotic tissue removed and everything drained (otherwise it may

progress towards deeper structures)

  • Drain left in place for 1-3 days to evacuate and avoid premature spontaneous closure
  • Local lavage with antiseptics is useful but high pressure must be avoided (risk of spreading bacteria to healthy tissue)
  • Antibiotics alone not sufficient BUT treatment must be started before surgical drainage
  • Bacterial infection contains colonic flora → Gram-negative and anaerobic bacteria (antibiogram !)
  • Sometimes it is so aggressive that it leads to Fournier gangrene

Fistula in anno

= hollow tract lined with granulation tissue, usually with proximal end at level of dentate line and distal one in perianal skin

  • Usually from perianal abscess after spontaneous drainage !
  • In complex fistulas → more than one distal opening

Associated conditions with complex fistula

  • CD
  • Diverticulitis
  • Local radiotherapy
  • Steroid therapy
  • HIV infection

Goodsall rule

= postulates that if the cutaneous opening is …

  • anterior → fistula will have a straight radial course to dentate line
  • posterior → fistula will be curved with internal opening on posterior midline

DD

  • Hydrosadenitis
  • Pilonidal sinus
  • Tuberculosis
  • Rectovaginal fistulae
  • Urethral-cutaneous fistulae

Symptoms

  • History of perianal abscesses followed by drainage of pus (slightly hemorrhagic and usually small volume)
  • Cutaneous orifice can close spontaneously → collecting of discharge, inflammation of surrounding tissue, after a

few days spontaneous reopening and evacuation of larger amount of puss

Diagnosis

  • DRE
  • Fistulography with iodine-contrast for recurrent cases and for mapping of complex fistulas
  • Endorectal US
  • CT (finds hidden abscesses)

Treatment

  • Classical surgical treatment = fistulectomy and/or fistulotomy
  • Fistulectomy = removes entire fibrotic tract by dissection of tract from skin to proximal opening, injecting a dye

through distal end can help to find the tract

  • Fistulotomy: canulation of fistula with probe, opening tract as wide as possible from one end to the other, part of

the sphincter situated between fistula and mucosa is also divided

  • This usually does not lead to incontinence, exception - elderly or recurrences of fistulae
  • Thus, it is prohibited to perform more than one fistulotomy at a time, otherwise incontinence cannot be avoided
  • Special fistulotomy: sequential ligatures or seton placement
    • Monofilament or rubber bands passed through fistula
    • First knot tied in surgery, others at 3-day intervals under local anesthesia
    • Last ligature cuts through tissue
    • Band acts as cutting and draining tool
    • Is applied in recurrences, complex fistulae, anterior fistulae in women, Crohn disease and elderly people with

low resting pressure

Seton placement

Pilonidal sinus

= cavity containing small amount of hair, pus, with walls lined with granulation tissue

  • Pathogenesis: formation of granulative tissue around hair that migrated tran-cutaneously (NOT hair growing

“inside” or in “wrong direction”)

  • Usually situated in midline of sacrococcygeal skin of hirsute young men
  • Definitive operative management consists frequently in simple excision without closure
  • Dye (methylene blue) is injected through sinus and entire capsule of fibrotic and granulation tissue is removed and

wound left to heal by secondary intention (healing may take 3-4 weeks)

  • Secondary suture after healthy granulative tissue fills gap/ whole

course.title: Rectal cancer
course.html:
Anatomy

  • Rectosigmoid junction between sigmoid colon and rectum
  • 15-17 cm from anal verge
  • Rectum 12-15 cm long and 4-16 cm from anal verge
  • Rectal tumors are < 16 cm from anal verge
  • Located at midpiece of sacrum (S3 vertebra)
  • Rectum is covered by peritoneum
  • on anterior surface and sides in upper 1/3
  • anterior surface only in middle 1/3
  • not covered in lower 1/3
  • It is divided into
  • Lower 0-6 cm from anal verge
  • Middle 7-11 cm
  • Upper 12-16 cm
Arteries- Superior Rectal Artery = main continuation of inferior mesenteric artery
- Middle Rectal Artery  (internal iliac artery = Hypogastric a.)
- Inferior Rectal Artery  (internal pudental artery)
Veins- Superior rectal vein → portal vein
- Middle rectal vein → inferior vena cava
- Inferior rectal v. (= inferior hemorrhoidal v.) → pudental v. → internal iliac v. → IVC
LymphaticsInferior- Superficial inguinal nodes
- Internal iliac nodes
Middle- The middle collecting lymph vessels drain into the internal Iliac chain
(= hypogastric lymph nodes) → Aortic lymph nodes
Superior- Lymphatic nodes accompanying origin of superior rectal artery (its
bifurcation or trifurcation = Mondor’s lymph nodes)
- Inferior mesenteric lymph nodes

Epidemiology

  • 2nd most frequent cancer of digestive tract (after gastric cancer); 60% of total large bowel tumors
  • More frequent in urban areas and developed countries (diet rich in fat and poor in fibers, higher life expectancy)
  • Most important risk factor: age (mainly after 50)
  • Maximum incidence 7th decade (60-69 years old), incidence begins to increase before 40
  • Men/Women = 9/5
  • Higher in African American populations and Ashkenazi Jewish
  • Most large bowel cancers occur in lower left side of colon near rectum-rectosigmoid junction
  • Synchronous tumor in 5 %
  • Metachronous tumors in 3-5 % (second tumor developing after resection of first)

Etiology

Diet- Diet rich in saturated fats
- Low-fiber diet
- Diet rich in smoked foods
- High alcohol intake
- Obesity, insulin resistance
- Smoking
Benign colonic tumors-Adenoma→ adenocarcinoma sequence in large bowel
Inflammatory bowel diseaseInflammatory bowel disease- A period of 10 - 15 years of latency
1. Ulcerative colitis (Colitis ulcerosa, UC)
2. Crohn's disease with rectal location
Radiation- Especially pelvis high dose radiation
- Tumors occur after a latency period of 10 years
Genetic factors- History of familial adenomatous polyposis
- Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome I and II)
- Acromegaly
- Personal history of colon, rectum, ovary, endometrium, breast CA
Surgical intervention on GI
tract		- Ureterosigmoidostomy (↑ risk of sigmoid neoplasm around stomy)
- Gastric surgery (Billroth I and vagotomies)
- Cholecystectomy (through increased biliary acids excretion)
- Colic resections
Protective factors
- Vit. D, folate, vitamins and antioxidants in fruit and vegetables, high fiber intake, low meat and animal fat
- Cruciferous vegetables (broccoli, cabbage)
- NSAIDs, aspirin
- Coffee
- Hormone replacement therapy
- Physical activity

Pathomorphology

Macroscopic- Proliferative, polypoid, exophytic
- Ulcerative
- Infiltrative-stenosing
- Combination
Microscopic- AdenoCA = most common → 95%
- Colloid (mucinous) CA
- Signet ring cell CA
- Undifferentiated CA
- Squamous cell CA
- carcinoid, GIST, sarcoma, melanoma, lymphoma

Clinical manifestation

  • Lower GI bleeding (often attributed to hemorrhoids, occult, fresh blood; black and tarry stools
  • Abdominal pain (pelvic and/or perineal)
  • Recent onset of bowel habits alteration (diarrhea and/or constipation)
  • Change in stool caliber = “crayon shaped stools” for inferior/ medium rectal tumors
  • Mucus discharge
  • Tenesmus
  • Sensation of incomplete evacuation
  • Anal incontinence → invasion of nerves or internal sphincter
  • When low back pain, locally advanced tumor should be suspected
  • 10% present with bowel obstruction
  • Weight loss, anorexia, asthenia, weakness, fatique

Complications

  • Bowel obstruction
  • Perforation; only for superior part of rectum; sometimes diastatic perforation
  • Fistula with urinary bladder/vagina/urethra
  • Hemorrhage
  • Rectal prolapse
  • Adjacent tissue invasion
  • Metastatic spread

Diagnosis

  • General physical examination: attention to inguinal lymph nodes, hepatomegaly, and jaundice
  • DRE: carcinomas belonging to inferior rectum → felt as hard mass, often ulcerated, with various degrees of

circumferential extent, mobile or fixed to surrounding tissues, bleed easily

  • If superior or middle rectal tumor → cannot be assessed digitally, but strings of blood or even stool sample may be

present on examination glove

  • RECTAL EXAM – COMPULSORY!

Lab analysis

  • CBC
  • Hb decreased → iron deficiency anemia
  • Leukocytosis
  • ALP, GGT increased → hepatic metastasis
  • Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) increased

Imaging

Total colonoscopy- Mandatory
- Biopsy + macroscopic aspect
- Be aware of synchronous cancer of colon !
- Determining distance between inferior margin of tumor and anal verge
→ determine whether anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection is needed
Anorectal/ Endorectal
US		- T and N staging: penetration of wall layers and nodal status
→ uT1: tumor confined to submucosa (not penetrating muscularis propria), with intact
bright middle hyperechoic layer (muscularis mucosa)
→ uT2: tumor invading muscularis propria with no disruption of third hyperechoic layer
→ uT3: tumor penetrating muscularis propria to involve perirectal fat and tissues, tumor
edge is usually irregular with disruption of 3rd hyperechoic layer (muscularis propria)
→ uT4: tumor invading an adjacent structure
- Overstaging occurs due to inflammatory reaction around carcinoma and differentiating
T2 lesions from T3 might sometimes become difficult
Abdominal US- Rectal tumor-superior
- Regional lymphadenopathy
- Hepatic metastasis > 1 cm in diameter
- Carcinomatous ascites
CT thorax, abdomen,- M staging
- Superior to abdominal US
pelvis
Pelvic MRIPelvic MRI= Golden standard
- High accuracy for rectal fascia propria invasion, distance from anal verge, presence of
adenopathy, evaluation of mesorectum
- Best for describing relationship between lesion, levator ani and sphincter
X-ray thorax- Pulmonary metastasis
PET scan- Suspicion of recurrence - or pulmonary metastasis
X-ray abdomen- Useful in emergency service (bowel obstruction or intestinal perforation)
Urography/cystoscopy- Fistulas or invasion
IrrigoraphySimple or double contrast; not routinely used

Screening

  • 5-year survival rate after resected colorectal cancer is 65%
Mild risk- Age, diet, physical inactivity, obesity, smoking, alcohol
→ Colonoscopy every 10 years after age 50
Intermediate risk- Personal history of colorectal cancer, strong family history
→ Colonoscopy every 3-5 years after age 40
High risk- Familial colorectal cancer syndromes
→ for familial polyposis after age of 10
→ for Crohn/ RCH with 10 years evolutions (annually)
→ for family history – 10 years before family member had cancer

DD

IBD- UC, CD, Radic rectitis
Rectal benign tumors- Polyp/ adenoma
- Teratoma
- Hemangioma
Secondary rectal tumors- Tumoral invasion from adjacent organs (ovaries, cervix, prostate)
- Gastric cancer pelvic metastasis (Blumer´s shelf)
Other rectal diseases- Rectal teleangiectasia
- Simple ulcer of rectum
- Ulcerations of venereal etiology
- Ischemic rectal colitis or stenosis
- Actinic stenosis
- Hemorrhoidal disease

Dissemination pathway

Direct pathwayProgressive “step-by-step” dissemination into adjacent tissue
- In axial direction
- Circumferential
- Into rectal wall thickness
-”frozen pelvis”
Lymphatic pathway- Superior rectal nodes → sigmoid nodes → inferior mesenteric nodes
- Internal iliac nodes (hypogastric nodes) → paraortic nodes
- Inguinal nodes (anal canal carcinoma)
Serous pathway- Via peritoneum, only for superior rectal tumors → peritoneal carcinomatosis
Venous pathwayVenous→ Superior rectal artery → portal vein → liver
→ Middle rectal veins → internal iliac vein → cave vein → lungs
→ Inferior rectal veins → external iliac vein → cave vein → lungs
Perineural spread

Sites of metastasis

Via blood- Liver, Lung, Brain, Bones
Via lymphatics- Lymph nodes
Per continuitatem- Abdominal wall
- Nerves
- Vessels

Tumoral grading

G1Well differentiated
→ Low grade
G2Moderately differentiated
G3Poorly differentiated tumors
G4G4Undifferentiated
→ High grade
= most aggressive

Tumor staging

  • ➔Astler-Coller staging system
Stage A- Limited to mucosa
- No lymph node involvement
Stage B1- Extending into muscularis propria
- No lymph node involvement
Stage B2- Penetrating through muscularis propria
- No lymph node involvement
Stage C1B1 + lymph node involvement
Stage C2B2 + lymph node involvement
Stage DDistant metastatic spread (liver, lungs, bone)
TNM staging
T
TTisCarcinoma in situ: intraepithelial or invasion of lamina propria
T1Tumor limited to mucosa (invades submucosa)
T2Tumor invades muscularis propria
T3T3Tumor invades through muscularis propria into subserosa/ pericolic/
perirectal tissues
T4Tumor directly invades other organs/ perforates
NN0No regional lymph nodes
N1Metastasis in 1-3 regional lymph nodes
N2Metastasis in > 4 regional lymph nodes
MM0No distant metastasis
M1Distant metastasis present
  • ➔Rectal cancer clinical stage grouping
Clinical stage
Stage IT1-2, N0M0
Stage IIT2-4, N0M0
Stage IIIT1-4, N+M0
Stage IVAny T, any N, M1

Treatment

  • 1) Surgical treatment
  • TNM determines local excision (T1), radical resection (T2) or neoadjuvant therapy (T3); nodal involvement (N+)

eliminates chance for curative local excision

  • radical/ palliative

Colon preparation methods

Fortrans solution method- Doesn’t get absorbed by intestinal wall
- Undegradable by intestinal flora
- 3-4 sachets of Fortrans get dissolved in 1 L of water each
- To be ingested the noon of the day preceding the surgical intervention
Fast-track method- Method currently used
- Enema preparation, previous evening and morning of surgery
- Antibiotics (cephalosporines + metronidazole), previous evening and morning of sur.
- Ingestion of 250 ml 10 % Glucose (morning of surgery)

Surgical treatment

Local excision

  • T1 only, N0, inferior rectum (within 8 cm from anal verge), well/ moderately differentiated, mobile and small tumor (< 3 cm), with no vascular or perineural spread
  • Transanal Endoscopic Microsurgery (TEM) - full-thickness excision with R0 margins, defects sutured
  • Complications are rare (urinary retention, hemorrhage, suture dehiscence, perirectal fat infection, rectovaginal fistulae)
  • Local recurrency possible (usually due to understaging or small positive lymph nodes (< 5 mm) usually not visible)

Radical resection

  • T1 (with high risk features), T2 and no nodal involvement → transabdominal resection is first line
  • Gold standard = total mesorectal excision (TME) - full rectal mobilization, preservation of urinary continence and sexual function (sparing hypogastric plexus and nervi erigentes), sharp dissection with free radial margins
  • Dissection of mesorectum 5 cm below inferior margin of tumor
  • Fixation of tumor to neighboring structures might be inflammatory
  • Unresectable if metastasis → colostomy might still be performed to avoid bowl obstruction
  • Middle rectal cancer: anterior resection and abdominoperineal resection possible
    • safety margin on 1-2 cm have to be achieved
  • In bowl obstruction → Hartmann’s resection (proximal colostomy and closure of rectal stump) offers possibility of tumor removal, time for tissue to heal and reestablishment of intestinal continuity usually after 6 months
  • Anastomosis requires good blood supply for both bowel ends and tension free technique; single or double layer suture or mechanical stapler; air test should be negative (air insufflated in distal rectum when pelvis is filled with saline)
  • Sometimes protective ileostomy, to decrease amount of contents going through anastomosis; reintegrated at a later date (6 weeks - 3 months), but it has not significantly decreased anastomotic leakage
  • In CRC → liver metastasis are always resected
I. Anterior resection
(Dixon procedure)		- Part of sigmoid colon and upper rectum removed
- Colo-rectal anastomosis
- Used for upper 2/3 of rectum cancer → at least 5 cm from anal verge !!!
II. Low anterior resection- Adequate resection margin
- Sphincter sparing
- Using linear and circular staplers
III. Ultra-low anterior resection- Right above dentate line
- Sphincter sparing
- Ultra-low colo-rectal or colo-anal anastomosis
- Using linear and circular staplers
- High risk of fistula !!!
IV. Abdomino-perineal resection
(Miles’ technique)		- Lower third of rectum → below 5 cm from anal verge !!!
- Wide perineal dissection
- Removal of anus, rectum and part of sigmoid colon
- End of remaining sigmoid colon is brought out permanently = colostomy
Laparoscopic surgery- Increased anatomical structures
- Perfect vision while performing deep pelvic dissection
- Minimal post-Op pain → less pain medication needed
- Short recovery and hospital stay
- Reduced risk of wound infections
- Reduced post-Op ileus
- Quick social reinsertion
- Faster administering of adjuvant therapy: ↑ survival rates over time
Significant associated risks
- Hemorrhage (most significant)
- Nerve lesions
- Reoccurence
- Fistulae
- Anastomotic stenosis

* Anastomosis is end-end or side-end +/- pouch

A. Anterior resection 76

B. Abdomino-perineal resection

a. anterior resection with colo-rectal anastomiosis

b. abdomino-perineal resection with permanent colostomy

  • 2) Radio-/ Chemotherapy
  • To lower recurrency and improve survival in resectable cancers
  • To allow surgery in primarily irresectable cancers
  • To facilitate a sphincter-preserving procedure
  • To cure patients without surgery: very small cancer or very high surgical risk
RadiotherapyMultiple chemotherapy
- Pre-OP (neoadjuvant): IIB - IV
- Post-OP (adjuvant treatment): I - II A
- Palliative: inoperable cases
- External radiation therapy→ linear particle accelerator
- Internal radiation therapy → local using iridium		Neoadjuvant – T3, N0 or any T, N1-2
Adjuvant
- If pathological finding after surgery equals T1-2, N0
→ no adjuvant therapy
- If pathological findings equals T3, N0 or T1-3, N1-2
→ adjuvant therapy
→ 5FU + levamisol
→ Irinotecan
→ Platinum salts
→ Vascular proliferation inhibitor
→ Epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitors (EGFRIs)
  • 3) Immunotherapy

Post-OP complications

  • Abdominal hemorrhage (occurs in first 24 hours)
  • Anastomotic leak (occurs in days 5-7 after surgery; higher rate of occurrence for low and ultra low anastomosis
  • Urinary retention
  • Postoperative ileus
  • Wound infection
  • Evisceration
  • Fecal incontinence
  • Anastomotic stenosis

Fast track protocol

  • Early oral nutrition, early ambulation, postoperative lower dosages of opioid analgesics and venous

thromboembolic prophylaxis have shortened postoperative ileus time and reduced length of hospital stay, accelerating patient recovery and contributing to health care budget savings

Surveillance

  • every 3-6 months for first 2 years
  • then every 6 months for total of 5 years
  • annual chest/abdomen/pelvis CT for patient at risk for recurrence
  • colonoscopy 1 year after operation, repeated every year if necessary

Colorectal CA prophylaxis

Primary prophylaxisSecondary prophylaxis
- Alimentary education
- NSAIDs → Aspirin, Sulindac		- Screening tests for precancerous polyps and incipient stages of cancer
- Hemocult tests – mandatory colonoscopy if positive
- Polyp diagnostic – endoscopic polypectomy
- Routine colonoscopy for people at risk
→ Inflammatory bowel disease
→ Offspring of individuals known with colorectal CA
→ Personal history of colon polyps
→ Molecular screening

Prognosis

  • Good survival rate
  • Stage IV with liver metastasis → 5-year survival rate 28-45%

book.html:
The rectum and anal canal Benign anal and perianal disorders

Ion Cosmin Puia

Hemorrhoids

The perianal veins exist in every healthy individual and play an important role in assuring continency for gas. In a very simple manner hemorrhoids (H) can be defined as varix of the ano-rectal veins. As a matter of fact they are arteriovenous plexuses. Ano-rectal veinous stasis plays a major role in the development of hemorrhoids. The engorged anal mucosa is easily traumatized, leading to rectal bleeding that is typically bright red due to high blood oxygen content within the arteriovenous anastomoses. Prolapse leads to soiling and mucus discharge (triggering pruritus) and predisposes to incarceration and strangulation.

The veins around the rectum constitute one of the porto-caval anastomosis. Any obstacle occurring in their area can lead to secondary hemorrhoids. This is the case for cirrhosis or large pelvic tumors. These must be ruled put before initiating any local treatment.

Dystrophic changes of the venous wall lead to essential or primitive hemorrhoids. The poor quality of the wall is the result of hereditary predisposal, local irritation and malnutrition. Classically, hemorrhoids were described more frequently in families with a background of hernia and varix of the lower limbs. Hemorrhoidal problems can be associated with inflammatory bowel disease, ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease. In pregnancy the ano-rectal complaints tend to aggravate. The cause can be the increased pressure due to the uterus but also specific hormonal changes. It seems that low-fiber diets cause small-caliber stools which lead to straining at defecation thus favorising the engorgement of the H. Reading on the toilet by impairing the venous return can be another cause of hemorrhoidal stasis.

The typical lesion is a venous dilation at the level of the hemorrhoidal plexus, situated between the superior hemorrhoidal vein and the middle and inferior hemorrhoidal veins. The former is part of the portal system and the latter of the inferior caval one. A cluster of veins composed by several dilations may be found at different levels. Those lying above dentate line are internal hemorrhoids and have a simple columnar epithelium. They also contain a subepithelial smooth muscle layer. Because they lack somatic sensory innervation internal H are painless. The external H develops beneath the dentate line, have a stratified squamous epithelium and receive somatic sensory innervation from the inferior rectal nerve. Mixed hemorrhoids combine internal and external hemorrhoids.

The evolution of the internal H can follow 4 stages, useful for prognosis and treatment:

  • Grade I can reach the anal canal during defecation without prolapse and bleed but do not prolapse.
  • Grade II hemorrhoids may protrude beyond the anal verge with straining or defecating but reduce spontaneously when straining ceases.
  • Grade III hemorrhoids protrude spontaneously or with straining and require manual reduction.
  • Grade IV hemorrhoids chronically prolapse and cannot be reduced. They usually contain both internal and external components and may present with acute thrombosis or strangulation.

The natural evolution of H begins with an anitis, sometimes subclinical. The inflammation of the mucosa spreads to the veins – the hemorrhoidal phlebitis. The affected veins dilate, get hypertrophic with a reflex contracture of the sphincter and irreducibility of the H. thrombosis follows as a rule. Other complications can follow:

* bleeding

* suppuration

* necrosis

* fissure

* ulcer

* phlebitis of the portal branches.

The spontaneous healing of the thrombosed H after the lysis of the clot transforms the H in a cutaneous flap.

Inspection with rectal exam should suffice for the diagnose. Yet flexible proctosigmoidoscopy is necessary to rule out inflammation or neoplasia. Pancolonoscopy is safer if the patient is older than 40 or symptoms are unspecific.

Usually symptoms can be relieved by better local hygiene, avoidance of excessive straining, and a balanced diet with fiber.

Suppositories and ointments containing cortisone should be avoided on long term basis.

Second degree H may benefit of more conservative techniques like rubber-band ligation, sclerotherapy, infrared photocoagulation, carbon dioxide freezing, heater probe, etc. Although considered the simplest and most effective and widely applied as an office procedure rubber band ligation can lead to severe perineal sepsis and even death.

Grade III and grade IV H, patients who fail nonoperative therapy and patients with significant symptoms hemorrhoidectomy is recommended. For simple thrombosed external hemorrhoids, excision in the office under local anesthesia is recommended immediately after the onset. Prior to surgery subacute bacterial endocarditis prophylaxis in valvular patients must be administered.

Ultrasonic scissors, bipolar electrocoagulation, laser can be used for the resection of the bundles. Usually three bundles are identified in the right anterior, right posterior, and left lateral positions. An operative retractor is useful and bridges of anoderm must be preserved to avoid the long-term complication of anal stenosis.

Fig.29: Longo technique – intraoperative view

Stapled hemorrhoid surgery (Longo technique) is the procedure of choice for prolapsed H. First described in 1997, it uses a modified circular stapler. A purse-string suture is placed with help of a plastic funnel-shaped device in the mucosa and submucosa above the dentate line beneath the anvil. The stapler is placed and closed. Excess hemorrhoid tissue is resected by the circular scalpel of the stapler. Hemostasis with interruption of the blood supply is ensured by the staple-line.

Annal fissure

The acute anal fissure is a radial tear affecting the epithelium of the anus. It is usually caused by the passage of a bulky, dehydrated piece of stool in constipated patients. Other causes can be iatrogenic, self-inflicted (foreign bodies), or trauma. The inflamed and fragile epithelium in diarrhea can also be affected by anal fissure.

The chronic fissure is a persistent ulcerous lesion with a granulation tissue-covered base and fibrotic margins. Sometimes the fibers of the internal anal sphincter are visible in the base of the chronic fissure. The posterior anal commissure is the most poorly perfused part of the anal canal. The typical chronic fissure is situated on the posterior midline (over 90%) and is usually hidden by a skin tag. It seldom occurs on the anterior midline. Other positions are exceptional and indicate that in these cases a sexually-transmitted disease must be considered. At anuscopy an inflamed papilla corresponds to the internal end of the anal fissure.

Other chronic lesions affecting the anus must be differentiated from the chronic fissure:

  • Crohn’s disease;
  • tuberculosis;
  • syphilis;
  • carcinoma.

The vicious circle pain-spasm-pain is associated with constipation because the patient tends to withhold defecation. Small bleedings may smear the surface of the stools or the toilet paper.

The physical exam is difficult because of the spasm. Topical application of 1-2% lidocaine gel and a gentle spreading of the anus can visualize the sentinel tag which hides the anal fissure. The rectal exam, sometimes unacceptable by the patient, will confirm the sphincter spasm.

The acute fissure usually heals without any special treatment. Local hygiene and avoiding constipation are sufficient. Chronic fissures however do not always respond to conservative measures. There are several local remedies meant to relieve spasm and thus facilitate the healing:

  • anesthetic gel;
  • a warm local bath 5 minutes before and after the defecation;
  • 0.2% nitroglycerin (NTG) ointment in the anal canal will also ameliorate the blood flow;
  • local injection of botulinic toxin bears the risk of recurrence after 3 month.

The surgical treatment has to solve both the spasm and the lesion itself. A gentle, progressive anal dilatation performed in spinal anesthesia, with duration of several minutes, must allow the insertion of the end of three fingers, but without tearing the fibers of the internal sphincter. The removal by electrocautery of the fibrotic tissue of the chronic fissure permits the later epithelisation of the fissure. The anal dilation procedure (Lord procedure), tends to be abandoned in favor of the partial lateral internal sphincterotomy.

The lateral internal sphincterotomy is also a pathogenetic orientated treatment because it reduces tension in the anus and allows the fissure to heal. The closed technique leaves the mucosa unharmed by inserting a thin scalpel between the sphincters and cutting only the internal component. Due to the elastic character of the sphincter the edges of the sphincterothomy retract leaving a palpable depression. The open technique starts with a segmental incision between the two sphincters.The internal is then dissected and radially cut.

In recurrent cases plastic procedures using flaps must be considered.

Perirectal (anorectal) Abscess

Perirectal suppurations arise from a cryptitis caused by the obstruction of the mucus-secreting anal glands, which drain into the anal crypts.

Depending on the direction of its progress and the anatomical spaces affected, the abscess is:

  • submucous;
  • ischiorectal;
  • pelvirectal;
  • horseshoeshaped
  • supralevator or pelvisubperitoneal.

Inflammatory signs can be easily observed in superficial abscesses: swelling, redness, tenderness and elevated temperature of the overlying skin. The first signs can be only perianal discomfort and pruritus.

Deep collections can alter the general status, with chills, fever, and nausea. The buttocks can be enlarged without obvious Celsian signs. The rectal exam can find a protrusion of the rectal wall. Pelvisubperitoneal abscesses can associate urinary signs and are particularly dangerous as they spread in contiguity to the retroperitoneal space.

Endorectal or vaginal ultrosonography or CT scan can be useful in deep-lying abscesses. Percutaneous punction and drainage may have a diagnostic purpose.

The drainage must not wait for the typical fluctuence because the abscess may progress towards deeper structures. A proper drainage can be performed only under spinal anesthesia. The cavity must be thoroughly explored digitally, necrotic tissue removed and loculations disrupted and drained. The drain must be left in place for 1-3 days to evacuate the discharges and avoid the premature spontaneous closure of the incision. Local lavage with antiseptics is useful but high pressure in instillation (especially in the case of hydrogen peroxide, which increases the intracavitary pressure by releasing gas) must be avoided because of the risk of spreading bacteria to healthy tissue.

Antibiotics alone, without surgical drainage, may attenuate the local and general signs, but do not solve the abscess. However, the antibiotic treatment must be started before the surgical drainage. The bacterial infection contains colonic flora so the choice treatment must be oriented towards Gram-negative and anaerobic bacteria. Sometimes the combination is so aggressive that it leads to Fournier gangrene, an extensive necrosis of the perineal soft tissues which can progress .The antibiogram is usually of little help, as in most cases the management allows to discontinue the AB treatment after 3 days. In special cases with an impaired immunity, the AB treatment must be continued for the necessary lapse of time.The patient must be warned of the risk of developing a perianal fistula.

Fistula in anno

Fistula in ano is a hollow tract, lined with granulative tissue, usually with the proximal end at the level of the dentate line and the distal one in the perianal skin. It usually continues the evolution of a perianal abscess, usually after a spontaneous drainage.

Although all fistulae in ano arise from a cryptithis, in some cases the proximal orifice cannot be found, the fistula being considered as blind. In complex fistulae it has more than one distal opening. It is frequently the case in patients with Crohn disease. Their treatment rarely gives satisfactory results and an attempt to surgically the fistula may worsen the local status. Other situations are associated with complex fistuae:

  • diverticulitis
  • local radiotherapy
  • steroid therapy
  • HIV infection.

Considering the passage through the anal sphincter fistulae after Parks classification system can be (fig.30):

  • intersphincteric
  • transsphincteric
  • suprasphincteric
  • extrasphincteric.

Fig.30: Fistula in anno – different variants

The Goodsall rule postulates that if the cutaneous opening is anterior to the frontal plane passing through the anus the F will have a straight radial course to the dentate line. If posterior to the plane the course will be curved with the internal opening on the posterior midline.

Fistula in ano must be differentiated from other suppurations involving the perianal tissue:

  • Hydrosadenitis;
  • Pilonidal sinus;
  • Tuberculosis
  • Rectovaginal fistulae;
  • Urethral-cutaneous fistulae.

The patient has a history of perianal abscesses followed by a remaining orifice with a discharge. The pus can be sometime slightly hemorrhagic and usually has a small volume (under 15ml). The cutaneous orifice can close itself spontaneously and leads to the collecting of the discharge, the inflammation of the surrounding tissue and, after a few days, to the spontaneous reopening and evacuation of a larger amount of puss.

At the rectal exam the fibrotic tract can sometimes be palpated. In recurrent cases a fistulography made by injecting iodine-contrast substances into the cutaneous orifice can be useful to obtain a map of a more complex fistula. An endorectal ultrosonography can identify cavities that can delay healing if not properly drained. The addition of hydrogen peroxide via the external opening can help outline the fistula tract course because the gas will enhance image of the tract.

The CT has the same purpose – to describe any abscess that communicates with the fistula. The classical surgical treatment consists in fistulectomy and/or fistulotomy. The fistulectomy removes the entire fibrotic tract by a step-by-step dissection of the tract, from the skin to the proximal opening at the level of the crypt. Injecting a dye through the distal end at a reasonable pressure can be helpful if the tract is lost during dissection. The proximal end can be identified during anuscopy more easily if dye or hydrogen peroxide is injected in the cutaneous orifice.

The canulation of the fistula with a probe can be helpful, especially for the fistulotomy. This consists of opening the tract as wide as possible, from one end to the other. In doing this the part of the sphincter situated between the fistula and the mucosa are also divided. Usually this does not lead to incontinence. An exception to this are the cases of the elderly or recurrences of fistulae, where this risk is higher so any preexistent such problems must be recorded.

It is totally prohibited to perform more than one fistulotomy at a time, otherwise incontinence cannot be avoided.

Fig.31: a. intraoperative view; b. same case, healed

A special fistulotomy can be performed using sequential ligatures or seton placement. After performing a partial fistulectomy on the cutaneous, superficial part of the tract, 3-4 ligatures are passed in the remaining part. Monofilament, silastic vessel markers, or rubber bands can be used, being better tolerated. The first knot is tied in surgery, the others at a 3 day interval, usually under local anesthesia. The last ligature usually cuts through the tissue; if not the remaining bridge of tissue can be cut with a scissor under local anesthesia. They act both as a scalpel and a drain, cutting, draining and guiding fibrosis. This technique is applied in recurrences, complex fistulae, anterior fistulae in women, Crohn disease and elderly people with low resting pressure.

The sealing of the tract with dual-component fibrin glue, after an initial enthusiasm, did not confirm the results on the long term.

A new technique uses a piece of collagen with an elongated conical shape that is placed in the fistula. The reticular structure of the collagen obtained from pig’s submucosa allows its colonization with fibroblasts. The inner orifice has to be sutured with a slowly absorbable suture. The success rate of this procedure is about 80%.

In any technique suspect tissue samples have to be biopsied.

Pilonidal sinus

The pilonidal sinus is a cavity containing a small amount of hair, pus, with walls lined with granulative tissue and is usually situated in the midline of the sacrococcygeal skin of hirsute young men. After the spontaneous evacuation after through a sinus (or incision) the apparent healing is followed, after several weeks, by the same abscess-like symptoms.

The pathogeny consists of the formation of granulative tissue around hair that migrated tran-cutaneously; it is not by hair growing “inside” or in the “wrong direction”. This was demonstrated of foreign hair (from a wig) being found inside the cavity. Also, similar abscesses were described on the chest of hairdressers which used to lean the head of their customers on that area.

The definitive operative management consists frequently in simple excision without closure. Dye (metilene blue)is injected through the sinus and the entire capsule of fibrotic and granulative tissue is removed and the wound left to heal by secondary intention. Another attitude is the per primam suture. Recurrence rates are lower if the wound is left open but the healing may take 3-4 weeks. A secondary suture after healthy granulative tissue fills the gap may be the best choice. Marsupialization, when wound edges are approximated to the sacral aponevrosis by “omega” shaped sutures may bare the same advantages but the scar is unaesthetic.

Rectal cancer

Florin Zaharie

Epidemiology

Epidemiologically, rectal cancer (RC) is analyzed along with colon cancer, having increased incidence and prevalence in more developed regions (probably due to diet rich in fat and poor in fibers and higher life expectancy) and higher mortality rates in less developed countries (due to advanced stages at the moment of diagnosis and limited treatment and follow-up resources). Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the 3rd most common cancer in men (10% incidence, after lung cancer and prostate cancer) and 2nd in women (9.2% incidence, after breast cancer) worldwide. Age is considered to be among the most important risk factors, 90% of cases are diagnosed after the age of 50; also, the risk increases with age. However, the incidence of CRC occurring before the age of 40 is increasing.There is no significant difference in incidence between the two sexes. Race and ethnicity seem to play a role in the development of CRC, the incidence is higher in African American populations compared to the Caucasian populations; the Ashkenazi Jewish individuals appear to be at a higher risk of developing CRC due to a more frequent gene mutation they inherit. There is also an increase in incidence in populations migrating from a lower risk region to a higher risk region.

Etiology

Diet has long been speculated to play an important role in the pathogenesis of CRC, but no studies have been able to state clearly which dietary components are responsible for the tumor development and which are protective. The carcinogenesis is a multistep process in which genetic susceptibility and external factors (such as dietary habits) intertwine. There have been many studies (observational, prospective, randomized trials) related to different dietary components intake, but none seem to draw the line and point out a certain constituent that drastically decreases or increases the risk for CRC development, mostly because one cannot have an exclusive diet based solely on one product. There are lifestyle trends regarding food intake such as people that consume more fruits, vegetables and fiber have less meat and fat in their diets and that might explain the decrease in CRC risk. The fibers accelerate the intestinal transit, reducing the contact between the carcinogens and colonic mucosa, also folate (DNA methylation), Calcium (precipitates bile acids), vitamin D (modulates Calcium absorption and has antiproliferative properties) were found to be associated with decreased CRC risk in some studies ; the antioxidants in fruit and vegetables are believed to have a protective effect, whereas the iron in red meat is a prooxidant and increases free radical production in the colon, causing mucosal damage. It can be stated, though, that an individual with no other CRC risk factors, having a diet rich in fiber, fruits and vegetables and poor in animal fat and red meat is at lower risk of CRC.

Obesity (insulin resistance), smoking, acromegaly, pelvic radiation, cholecystectomy, ureterosigmoidostomy are considered to be risk factors for CRC. Higher alcohol intake (reduces folate absorption and interferes with DNA normal methylation) is also associated with increased CRC risk. There is evidence of the protective effect of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) including aspirin, though the antineoplastic mechanisms are incompletely understood. NSAIDs users have a significantly decreased risk of CRC and a lower cancer-specific mortality rates (in patients with history of CRC), but chemoprophylaxis with these agents was found not to be cost-effective and is outweighed by the appearance of gastrointestinal complications. Hormone replacement therapy and physical activity decrease CRC risk.

People at risk for developing CRC have personal history of adenoma or sessile serrated polyps, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), CRC in the past or family history (especially 1st degree relatives) of CRC; high risk syndromes (Lynch syndrome, polyposis syndromes) require active surveillance.

Carcinogenesis is a multi-step process; it needs the accumulation of both inherited and acquired genetic mutations to become clinically manifest. In the case of sporadic CRC, several gene mutations contribute to the transformation of colorectal normal epithelium into adenoma and, later on, into carcinoma (Fig.32).

Surgical Anatomy

The rectum is the last portion of the large bowel. It begins at the level of the sacral promontory and ends at the anal verge; it measures 12-15 cm in length and lacks a mesentery, sacculations, and appendices epiploicae. It is divided into three equal parts: the upper third, which is mobile and has a peritoneal coat except near the middle third where the peritoneum only covers the anterior and part of the lateral surfaces; the middle third - confined to the bony pelvis; the lower third, lying within the muscular floor of the pelvis.

The superior rectal artery is the direct continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery and is the main arterial supply of the rectum. The middle rectal artery arises on each side from the internal iliac artery and approaches the rectum through the lateral ligaments. Inferior rectal artery comes from the internal pudendal artery and supplies the anal canal distal to the pectinate line.

The rectum is drained by the superior rectal veins, which enter the inferior mesenteric veins draining into the portal system. The middle and inferior rectal veins enter the internal iliac vein draining into the systemic circulation.

Above the pectinate line, lymphatic drainage is to the inferior mesenteric nodes; below the line, lymphatic drainage goes to the inguinal lymph nodes.

Clinical features

The patient with rectal cancer most commonly presents to the doctor for lower GI bleeding (often attributed to hemorrhoids), abdominal pain (pelvic and/or perineal, depending on the location of the tumor), recent onset of bowel habits alteration (diarrhea and/or constipation), weight loss (without obvious reasons), anorexia. Other signs and symptoms include change in the stool caliber, mucus discharge, tenesmus, sensation of incomplete evacuation. When low back pain is associated, locally advanced tumor should be suspected. Almost 10% of the patients present with bowel obstruction.

The general physical examination is essential for the surgeon, offering important information about the extent of local disease and the presence of metastases; attention should be paid to liver, the inguinal lymph nodes and if jaundice is present. On digital rectal examination, if there is a carcinoma belonging to the inferior rectum, it can be felt as a hard mass, often ulcerated, with various degrees of circumferential extent, mobile or fixed to the surrounding tissues (anteriorly it may invade the vagina wall or prostate, posteriorly – the sacrum), it may also bleed easily to the touch. If the tumor belongs to the superior or middle rectum, it cannot be assessed digitally, but strings of blood or even stool sample may be present on the examination glove. Along with the imaging techniques and laboratory blood work, the physical examination allows the clinician to contour the therapeutic plan and act accordingly.

Differential diagnosis of rectal cancer includes internal hemorrhoids, benign rectal polyps, ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease, ischemic colitis, radiation proctitis, invasive prostate cancer.

Investigations

If rectal cancer is suspected in a patient (whether because of the symptoms or after physical examination), colonoscopy is mandatory: to macroscopically characterize the tumor, to biopsy the lesion and to assess the remaining colon for the presence of synchronous neoplasia.

Rigid sigmoidoscopy is useful for determining with accuracy the distance between the inferior margin of the tumor and the anal verge. This will determine whether an anterior resection or an abdominoperineal resection is needed.

All patients should undergo a chest X-ray examination in order to detect possible pulmonary metastases and to assess the pulmonary status.

Endorectal ultrasound (ERUS) describes the depth of penetration of the tumor in the rectum wall layers and the nodal status. It has comparable accuracy as pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), especially for the lower rectal tumors. Overstaging occurs due to the inflammatory reaction around the carcinoma and differentiating T2 lesions from T3 might sometimes become difficult. As any US technique, it is user dependent and accuracy of description increases with experience of the examiner. ERUS is best for describing T1 tumors for which transanal excision is proposed.

MRI can accurately predict rectal fascia propria invasion. The involvement of the circumferential resection margin is a predictor of local recurrence and this may require neoadjuvant therapy (for downstaging purposes) and extensive resection. Also, in patients with low rectal tumors that will undergo sphincter-preserving procedures, MRI is better for describing the relationship between the lesion, levator ani and the sphincter complex.

Computed tomography (CT) with i.v. and/or oral contrast is a common method to evaluate loco-regional and distant spread, although MRI and Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography (FDG-PET) are significantly more accurate. High resolution technology, such as the multidetector-row computed tomography (MDRCT), might improve CT results regarding depth of invasion and lymph node involvement.

FDG-PET has higher sensitivity and specificity than CT or MRI in detecting recurrent rectal carcinoma after curative surgery, but lower specificity for tumor location. Therefore, hybrid methods (such as PET/CT) have been conceived to surpass this inconvenience.

With regard to the blood panel, blood count could reveal anemia, altered liver function tests (rises suspicion of metastatic disease), leukocytosis (in tumor abscesses), elevated carcino-embryonic antigen (CEA). This marker was most studied, but does not have enough sensitivity and specificity to represent a screening test; values are measured after the initiation of the treatment in order to appreciate the recurrence of the disease.

Classification. Staging

The staging system has been introduced in 1930 (modified in 1932) by Charles Dukes to better guide the clinician towards the best course of treatment and to have an accurate prognosis. Since then, changes have been made to this classification (best known is the Modified Astler-Coller – MAC classification), but currently most of the clinics use the TNM staging system (latest version is the 7th edition of the American Joint Committee on Cancer). It describes the primary tumor development (T), the nodal involvement (N) and the presence of distant metastasis (M).

Pathology

Most common rectal malignant neoplasia is the adenocarcinoma (90-95%); other malignancies include signet ring carcinoma (with worse prognosis), squamous cell carcinoma, carcinoid, GIST, sarcoma, melanoma, lymphoma.

Macroscopically, there are 4 types of tumors: ulcerative (most frequent; can invade all the layers), polypoid (protrudes in the lumen; usually it is not invasive), annular (circumferential evolution; leads to bowel obstruction); infiltrating (covered by intact mucosa; higher mortality and worse prognosis).

There was no correlation found between the size of the tumor and the prognosis.

On a microscopic level, there are 4 grades of tumor differentiation, regarding the amount of glandular tissue present within: G1 (well differentiated), G2 (moderately differentiated), G3 (poorly differentiated), G4 (undifferentiated). Poorly differentiated and mucinous histologic patterns are associated with poor prognosis, but the two most important prognostic factors are depth of invasion and the presence of lymph node metastases. If a tumor has islets with different grades, the greater will be considered as defining the lesion.

Mechanisms of spread for rectal carcinoma involve: direct extension (into the thickness of the bowel wall), transperitoneal spread, implantation of malignant cells lower on a pre-existing mucosal lesion (hemorrhoidectomy, fistulectomy), lymphatic spread (following perirectal nodes and via superior rectal artery), venous spread (leading to distant metastases).

Management

Appropriate course of treatment requires rigorous patient selection. Preoperative staging will establish which patient is candidate for local excision (T1), surgical resection (T2) or neoadjuvant therapy (T3); nodal involvement (N+) eliminates the chance for a curative local excision.

Local excision with curative intent can be performed on a restricted group of patients: T1 only, N0, inferior rectum (within 8 cm from anal verge), well/ moderately differentiated, mobile and small tumor (< 3 cm), with no vascular or perineural spread. Resection margins should be all free of tumor cells. Transanal techniques require full-thickness excision (all layers of the bowel wall) until the perirectal fat becomes visible. The bowel defect is then sutured transversely in a fashion the surgeon prefers.

In the early 1980’s the TEM (Transanal Endoscopic Microsurgery) technique was developed. It offers the surgeon access to all rectal length and space to perform elaborate dissection (using 5 mm instruments); also, it allows the removal of larger lesions. Complications are rare (urinary retention, hemorrhage, suture dehiscence, perirectal fat infection, rectovaginal fistulae), but may require a new intervention and sometimes a diversion ostomy.

Local recurrence after local excision is detected if thorough follow-up is performed and should be promptly surgically sanctioned. Many of these cases are rather Stage III under-staged lesions, than real recurrences after Stage I tumor removal. This occurs due to small positive lymph nodes (< 5 mm) usually not visible using imaging techniques. New ways of marking these nodes based on their metabolism are being developed, but are not currently in clinical use.

Surgical radical resection has higher morbidity and mortality rates than the local excision, but along with chemoradiation therapy offers selected cases the chance of a curative treatment. When taken into consideration, surgical resection should achieve 4 major goals: tumor removal in its entirety, with negative margins (R0 resection); restoration of anatomy (whenever is possible); minimization of functional impairment; assuring the best quality of life possible.

For clinical T1 (with high risk features), T2 and no nodal involvement, transabdominal resection is the first line treatment. If the pathological finding is equal to the preoperative staging (pT1-2, N0), there is no need for adjuvant therapy, only surveillance. If the pathological exam finds a pT3, N0 or pT1-3, N1-2 specimen (meaning the tumor was more advanced than the investigations showed and/or there were positive lymph nodes), adjuvant therapy is advised.

The gold standard for rectal cancer surgery is the total mesorectal excision (TME), introduced by Heald in the early 1980's. Since then, survival rates have dramatically improved and the local recurrence rates have significantly decreased.It allows full rectal mobilization, preservation of urinary continence and sexual function (sparing hypogastric plexus and nervi erigentes) and due to sharp dissection it offers better chance to a tumor-free radial margin. Dissection of the mesorectum is to be made 5 cm below the inferior margin of the tumor.

Preoperative bowel preparation (using various methods: liquid diet several days before surgery plus enema, laxatives, mannitol solution,saline irrigation through nasogastric tube or polyethylene glycol solution) was introduced in order to reduce fecal flora, to better visualize the lumen during surgery and it was believed to prevent anastomotic and infectious complications. Studies have shown there is no significant difference between patient with and without preoperative bowel preparation. Some studies even showed an increase in anastomotic leaks rate. The choice is in the hands of the surgeon whether he prefers bowel preparation before the surgery or not.

Antibiotic prophylaxis, either by oral antibiotics, intravenous antibiotics or both, is performed the day before surgery; it decreases the risk ok postoperative septic complications. Commonly used antibiotics: metronidazole, erythromycin, neomycin.

The operability of a patient is decided by the surgeon taking into account the general status, the stage of the disease and whether the lesion can or cannot be safely removed. On the other hand, the resectability of a tumor is ultimately assessed intraoperatively considering the presence of hepatic or peritoneal metastases; fixation of the tumor might be of inflammatory origin. An unresectable case (for example frozen pelvis) may still benefit from a diverting colostomy in order to avoid bowel obstruction.

For the upper third of the rectum, the choice of surgical treatment is low anterior resection (A), whereas abdominoperineal resection (B) is an option for the lower third of the rectum (fig.33). There are surgeons pushing the limits of low anterior resection to ultra-low resection, advocating for sphincter-sparing methods (ultra-low colorectal or colo-anal anastomosis). These procedures are feasible using devices such as linear and circular staplers. The quality of life for these patients is significantly superior to the ostomy patient and abdominoperineal resection is advised to be performed when achieving negative distal margin is questionable, the tumor invades the anal sphincter or anal incontinence was present before surgery.

For the middle third of the rectum both anterior resection and abdominoperineal resection constitute an option, depending on various factors: general status, obesity, lesion level, size and stage, grade, presence of complications (perforation, abscess, obstruction). As long as a distal margin of 2 cm can be achieved, low anterior resection remains a valid option for mid and low rectal cancers.

For patients presenting with bowel obstruction due to a rectal cancer complete stenosis, Hartmann’s resection (proximal colostomy and closure of the rectal stump) offers the possibility of tumor removal with patient stabilization and reestablishment of intestinal continuity for second intent (usually after 6 months).

The approach can be either open or laparoscopically assisted, depending on the surgeon’s experience and on the particularities of the case. The anastomosis (when performed) may be single or double-layer hand sewn (with running or interrupted sutures) or mechanical (using staplers). Rules for a successful anastomosis and to avoid risk of anastomotic leakage: good blood supply for both bowel ends, tension-free technique (even if it involves mobilization of splenic flexure); when surgeon opts for a mechanical anastomosis, the tissue rings coming off the circular stapler should be complete and air-test should be negative (after the anastomosis is performed, air is insufflated in the distal rectum when pelvis is filled with saline). Some surgeons prefer a protective ileostomy, to decrease the amount of contents going through the anastomosis (which is reintegrated at a later date, usually 6 weeks to 3 months), but it has not significantly decreased the anastomotic leakage rate, involving operative, postoperative and anesthetic risks.

For clinical T3, N0 or any T, N 1-2 neoadjuvant treatment is recommended (chemoradiation protocols) before transabdominal resection. If the tumor is advanced (T4) and/or unresectable at initial evaluation, chemoradiation is indicated at first; if it becomes resectable, surgical removal may be taken into consideration with proper adjuvant therapy.

The incidence of synchronous large bowel cancers is approx. 3.5%. In this case, careful preoperative planning is necessary, opting for the best and least traumatic combination of resections.

Locally advanced rectal cancer may require resection of tissue belonging to the invaded organs (uterus, small intestine, urinary bladder, prostate), provided that margins are tumor free. Surgeon can opt for resection with curative intent or a palliative resection, depending on the preoperative thorough evaluation.

Recurrence rates ranges from 12 to 50% depending on the initial stage. Locoregional recurrence incidence has decreased in the last 3 decades due to the introduction of TME in surgical practice. Recurrent rectal carcinoma may still benefit from resection with curative intent, if promptly discovered. Most common site of distant recurrence is the liver.

Almost 20% of patients present with stage IV disease. Attentive oncologic planning offers these patients relatively high survival rates if managed properly. Liver metastases, if suitable for resection, can be excised at the same time as the primary tumor removal or at a later date (performance status and comorbidities taken into account). Other treatment options for liver metastases include hepatic artery infusional chemotherapy, radiofrequency ablation (RFA) and microwave ablation (MWA), cryotherapy. Re-resection of liver metastases can be performed with curative intent in carefully selected cases. Pulmonary metastasectomy is feasible, even with synchronous liver resection, but overall offers a poor prognosis.

The extent of peritoneal carcinomatosis is a major prognostic factor. In this case, removal of primary tumor and associated chemotherapy offers longer period of disease control. Recently, cytoreductive surgery (removal of peritoneal tumor deposits) and intraperitoneal chemotherapy have gained ground, but due to the high costs of the treatment and the lack of large clinical trials they are not commonly used in clinical practice. Rectal cancer can also metastasize to the ovaries, bones or brain.

Metastatic disease significantly shortens the survival interval, but new course of treatment is arising, offering stage IV patients better treatment options.

Fast track protocols (early oral nutrition, early ambulation, postoperative lower dosages of opioid analgesics and venous thromboembolic prophylaxis) have shortened the postoperative ileus time and reduced the length of hospital stay, accelerating patient recovery and contributing to health care budget savings.

Screening, Surveillance

Screening tests for average risk population (age over 50, negative personal or family history of CRC) requires colonoscopy (repeated after 10 years if negative) and/or stool testing (repeated after 1 year if negative). People with high risk of developing rectal cancer should undergo active surveillance with more frequent testing.

Surveillance after surgical treatment implies physical examination and CEA determination (for T2 or greater) every 3 to 6 months for the first 2 years and then every 6 months for a total of 5 years; annual chest/abdomen/pelvis CT for patient at risk for recurrence; colonoscopy 1 year after the operation (repeated in 1 year, if necessary).

Survival rates differ according to race (USA overall 5-year survival rate for Caucasians was 67% and for African Americans - 59%, respectively), stage at diagnosis, neoadjuvant/adjuvant treatment, palliative/curative treatment etc.

These figures come from people treated with various techniques at different moments (some many years ago). As cancer treatment continues to improve, survival rates become higher. Stage IV patients with curative liver treatments have an encouraging 5-year survival rate ranging from 28% to 45%, whereas left untreated, survival rates for patients with liver metastases are 2-8%.

For Tis (stage 0) and for selected T1 cases, 5-year survival rates tend to reach 100%.

Neoadjuvant and adjuvant treatment

Chemotherapy and radiation have increased survival rates and disease-free intervals.Usually, chemotherapic protocols involve the use of 5 Fluorouracil, leucovorin, capecitabine, irinotecan and platinum-based drugs; can be used prior and/or after the surgery. Radiotherapy is mostly used before the surgery, although there are studies showing lower recurrence rates after adjuvant radiation in comparison to neoadjuvant radiation; it downstages the tumor and offers better local control, but induces radiation enteritis, cystitis. Palliative radiotherapy offers pain relief, diminishes bleeding and diarrhea. Both chemotherapic agents (Heated Intraperitoneal Chemotherapy – HIPEC, associated with cytoreductive surgery) and radiation (Intraoperative Electron Beam Radiotherapy - IOERT) are used during surgery in clinical trials in search for the best multimodality treatment combination for the patient.

Complications

Patients with rectal cancer may present in the Emergency Department with lower GI bleeding, acute abdomen (in case of tumor perforation or bowel obstruction) in which case the surgeon may adopt an aggressive attitude (resection, if technically possible and if the status of the patient allows) or a prudent approach (palliative ostomy, with patient stabilization) and second intent resection. Other non-invasive ways of managing rectal obstruction include laser therapy, fulguration and placement of self-expanding stent.

During surgery, incidents may happen: spleen injury, presacral plexus hemorrhage, ureter or urinary bladder injury.

Postoperatively, patient may experience abdominal hemorrhage (occurs in the first 24 hours), anastomotic leak (occurs in days 5-7 after the surgery; higher rate of occurrence for low and ultra-low anastomosis; risk factors: anemia, male sex, age over 65, cardiovascular and pulmonary comorbidities, hypoproteinemia with hypoalbuminemia), urinary retention, postoperative ileus, wound infection, evisceration. Later complications that may occur: fecal incontinence, anastomotic stenosis.

In conclusion, rectal cancer is a potentially curable disease, with numerous treatment options as long as it is caught in time. The best oncologic results are achieved in high-volume institutions and if operations are performed or supervised by experienced surgeons. Laparoscopic approach for cancer patients is gaining more ground, making radical interventions minimally invasive. Survival rates are getting higher with the prospects of new chemotherapic regimens and targeted radiation, but surgery still remains the cornerstone of the curative treatment for rectal cancer.
